questions_asked:
# Expert Question 1 (Operator 1: open-ended)

I am modeling the 2018 MCM Problem A: a 100-W constant-carrier HF signal (below MUF)
from a land source, first reflected once by the ionosphere then once by the ocean
(turbulent vs calm), followed by additional calm-ocean hops, with a 10 dB usable-SNR
cutoff. The problem statement fixes none of the following structural quantities, and each
one is required to parameterize the core mechanism:

(a) The geometry convention for "hops". Is the counting intended as:
    (i) a skywave path of n successive ionospheric hops, where every ionospheric hop
        lands on the ocean and takes one ocean-surface reflection (so the first ocean
        reflection belongs to the first ionospheric hop, as the note "one reflection off
        the ionosphere" suggests), or
    (ii) alternating ground-wave/ionospheric segments in which "n reflections off the
        ocean" is counted as n discrete sea-surface bounces independent of skywave count?
    The usable-hop count and the first-reflection strength both depend on which reading
    is meant, because (i) ties every ocean reflection to an ionospheric absorption pass.

(b) The definition of "first reflection off the ocean" strength: the power density at
    the sea surface just before the sea bounce (i.e., after the ionospheric hop and all
    free-space losses), the power density just after the sea bounce (reflection
    coefficient applied), or the received power at the eventual distant ground point
    after the next ionospheric hop? Which of these is the quantity the "compare
    turbulent vs calm" clause is meant to compare?

(c) The domain of validity for the ocean-reflection treatment: is the model expected to
    operate at high (grazing) incidence over long paths — where a flat, lossy-sea
    Fresnel coefficient plus a roughness (Rayleigh) attenuation factor is the correct
    limit — or is it expected to span near-vertical incidence at short ranges, where the
    roughness treatment and the Fresnel limit both change? In other words, what is the
    valid (incidence angle, range, frequency) domain the judge should expect the
    reflection model to cover, and is a single-frequency, single-path (great-circle,
    mid-latitude) treatment the intended scope for Parts I–III?

I am not asking for magnitudes or empirical constants (seawater permittivity, MUF, and
ionospheric absorption are fixed by the supplied literature lookups). I am asking only
for the logical boundary of each quantity: which reading of (a)–(c) makes the rest of
the problem internally consistent, so that the model's variables, the hop-counting, and
the SNR budget all attach to the same definition of a "hop".

# Expert Question 2 (Operator 2: judgment)

Building on your answers — reading (i) for hop counting, the post-sea-bounce power
density as the comparison quantity, and the grazing-incidence / flat-Fresnel-times-
Rayleigh-roughness domain — I propose the following structural allocation for the signal
budget. Please accept or reject it as a whole (I do not ask you to choose among
alternatives).

Per one hop i (one ionosphere-ocean-ionosphere cycle), the received power density after
the sea bounce is

  S_i = S_{i-1} × (1/R_i^2) × A_io(f) × |Γ_sea(f, θ_i, surface_i)|^2 × A_io(f),

where:
  1. (1/R_i^2) is the two-way free-space spreading over the hop length R_i (isotropic
     source, 100 W constant carrier);
  2. A_io(f) ≤ 1 is the one-way ionospheric absorption+scattering factor, applied once
     on the way down and once on the way up, with f = 0.85 × MUF the nominal operating
     frequency (per the supplied lookup item 2);
  3. |Γ_sea|^2 is the squared sea-surface reflection coefficient:
       - calm ocean: flat, lossy-medium Fresnel coefficient |Γ_calm|^2 at grazing
         incidence, computed from the seawater complex permittivity (lookup item 1);
       - turbulent ocean: |Γ_calm|^2 × exp(−4π σ_h cos θ_i / λ)^2, i.e. the same Fresnel
         coefficient times a Rayleigh roughness factor with rms height σ_h, applied only
         to the first (turbulent) sea bounce; hops 2..n are calm by the problem's terms.

The multi-hop usable count is then the largest n such that
  S_n / N_0 ≥ 10 dB
with N_0 the receiver noise floor (kTB, T ≈ 290 K, B the receiver bandwidth), and the
comparison in Part I is the ratio Γ_turb/Γ_calm in dB, computed at the first bounce.

Specifically I put to you: (1) is applying the Rayleigh factor as a multiplicative
attenuation on |Γ|^2 — rather than as an extra path loss in the (1/R^2) term — the
correct structural placement for the turbulent contrast; and (2) is the two-way
application of A_io per hop (down-leg and up-leg separate, each with its own
absorption) the correct phase organization of the per-hop loss, given that the
ionospheric pass is the part of the mechanism the supplied data can support
(lookup item 2 gives absorption order, not a constant)?

# Expert Question 3 (Operator 3: counterexample)

You rejected my Exchange-2 allocation, so I will run the fallback standard structure:
one ionospheric (round-trip) loss pass per hop, one-way free-space spreading per leg,
the flat-lossy-sea Fresnel coefficient times a Rayleigh roughness factor applied only to
the first (turbulent) sea bounce, calm-ocean Fresnel coefficient for hops 2..n, and the
usable-hop count as the largest n with S_n/N_0 ≥ 10 dB (N_0 = kTB, T = 290 K).

Which specific case, boundary condition, or failure mode breaks this mechanism? In
particular, I want you to identify (a) the regime in which the Rayleigh
exp(−(4πσ_h cosθ/λ)²) factor stops being a valid model of the turbulent contrast
(e.g. when σ_h cos θ approaches λ/2 and the surface is no longer "rough" in the
Rayleigh sense, so coherent backscatter is lost and diffuse scattering dominates), and
(b) the boundary condition on hop geometry (e.g. hop length so short that the sea-surface
incidence angle leaves the grazing regime, or MUF so low that 0.85×MUF drops the signal
into a frequency band where ionospheric absorption is no longer "small, order tenths of
dB" per the supplied lookup) at which the per-hop loss budget I described stops
representing the actual mechanism. One concrete boundary condition for each is enough;
I will state both in the limitations/bias section of the report.
expert_answers:
(a) Reading (i): each hop is one ionosphere-to-ocean-to-ionosphere cycle, so the first ocean reflection belongs to the first ionospheric hop. This makes the hop count, the ocean-reflection count, and the SNR budget attach to one segment definition.

(b) The quantity compared is the power density just after the sea bounce — incident density after the ionospheric hop and free-space spreading, multiplied by the sea reflection coefficient. That isolates the ocean surface as the variable under test; comparing at the eventual ground point would fold in a second ionospheric absorption pass and confound the turbulent-vs-calm contrast.

(c) The intended domain is high-frequency, grazing-incidence, long-path skywave: flat lossy-sea Fresnel coefficient times a Rayleigh roughness attenuation factor, single frequency, single great-circle mid-latitude path. Near-vertical, short-range incidence lies outside the scope the problem's hop mechanism presumes.

(a) The Rayleigh factor breaks when the surface is no longer slightly rough: once σ_h cos θ approaches λ/(4π) — not λ/2 — the coherent (specular) component is already strongly suppressed, and beyond the Rayleigh criterion σ_h cos θ ≳ λ/8 the return is dominated by diffuse/incoherent scattering, so a single multiplicative attenuation on |Γ|² no longer represents the turbulent contrast.

(b) The grazing-incidence boundary: when the hop length is short enough that the sea-surface incidence angle departs grazing (θ above roughly 10–15° from the surface), the flat-Fresnel grazing limit and the roughness factor both cease to apply, and the per-hop budget no longer describes the mechanism.
